Tratto dal ponderoso romanzo di Paulo Lins (600 pagine), il film risulta fallimentare sotto tutti i punti di vista. Perché se è vero che le favelas di Rio de Janeiro rappresentano il luogo di un degrado sociale e morale certo profondo e di non facile soluzione, è altrettanto vero che non è con questa operazione che si può sperare di portare un minimo aiuto alla causa. Non risparmiando niente sul piano visivo per quanto attiene a brutalità e violenze e anzi lasciandole uniche, incontrastate protagoniste, il regista vorrebbe far passare l'idea che lui si limita a riprendere la realtà senza intervenire: ma l'eccesso di realismo scavalca il confine della credibilità e fa diventare il racconto più finto della finzione. Dominano allora personaggi come macchiette in mezzo ad un quadro di vita che non restituisce mai la complessità della situazione, essendo insisitito in una sola direzione, quella del crimine e della perdita della vita da adolescenti. Parziale e nichilista, il film accumula solo sconcezze e volgarità, compiacendosi di mostrare bambini sempre più piccoli in giro per le strade pronti ad uccidere, e così impedendo di mettere in piedi qualunque riflessione su quelle situazioni gravi che si vorrebbero (forse, ma non è sicuro) denunciare. Dal punto di vista pastorale, il film è da valutare come inaccettabile, e fortemente negativo.

I honestly don’t understand the overwhelming praise for City of God. While the film has impressive camera work and a fast-paced style, I found it exhausting rather than engaging. The constant violence, brutal characters, and endless cycle of crime make it feel more like a long sequence of shocking moments than a meaningful story. The characters are difficult to connect with because so many of them are defined by cruelty and survival, leaving little emotional depth for the audience to hold on to. The movie seems more interested in showing chaos and brutality than exploring the people behind it. The storytelling style, with its rapid editing and nonstop narration, can also feel distracting and overcomplicated. Instead of creating a powerful emotional experience, it sometimes feels like the film is trying too hard to prove how gritty and intense it can be. Although it has technical strengths, City of God was not an enjoyable watch for me. It is violent, overwhelming, and far too focused on misery to be the masterpiece many people claim it is. DONT RECOMMEND WATCHING

Can we actually find value in a film that while yes shows the violence people go through when their material needs aren’t met, but doesn’t actually fully call out the cause of the violence? I don’t think so. Especially when the violence towards the men, women, and children is shown as just a symptom and not actually done tactfully. To not have any discussion about the cause of the violence is because of state and police violence, because of class systems, racism, and sexism is irresponsible. Vague pointing at police is not enough. This film says violence begets violence and that right there is the most violent part of this film. These people deserve more. And if all we do is witness the violence can we say we are any better? I don’t think so.

I can’t imagine many of the people who live in The City Of God at the time actually saw this theatrically. And I imagine they would find this distasteful. This is all quite gauche and feels exploitative of real poverty and the trap of poverty. The film deals with race quite strangely as well in a way that made me feel a little bit uncomfortable. Im not really a fan of the style of this either, it’s all very flashy but it kind of makes the characters never feel fully realised. They don’t feel like real people because the movie is more interested in being stylised poverty porn exploitation than a story about people. The idea of gazing at disproportionally black poverty and violence and killing is not interesting to me. Especially when it isnt made for or by the community it is depicting the suffering of. The way death and dead bodies are handled in this film intentionally lacks a level of weight i think to alienate people and upset them. But an image  containing only viscera  divorces the humanity of death and turns it into a spectacle to gaze at. If this came out in an English speaking environment i think people would be more critical of this. Most English speaking audiences don’t really watch films in other languages. I think there is an element of this being an incredibly easy to understand narrative and stylistically familiar enough that more people would give this a shot as a “foreign film”. Which i think lends to a level of exoticism to how some people interact with and engage with the film. Of the few negative reviews i have bothered glancing at a lot of them seem to come from Brazil. There are other crime films i share this criticism with. However there are still several crime films that feel connected enough to the communities depicted in them, to where I feel they are less problematic. The gaze and regard in which this film is held in to me reads as somewhat colonial. The Auteurs and audience domination and extraction of respect, life and humanity in exchange for a narrative that allows people to have their “Harrowing” movie where they get to watch vicariously through an audience surrogate. Where is the framework of media analysis with the response to this film? I genuinely think audiences collectively should scrutinise this film so much more. During my film course at uni there have been several films we have seen where we interrogate how we felt about the film we just watched, we process what it was saying, what it meant, and even at times analysed where the point of view of its conception came from. And sometimes this encompassed the ethics of a film’s conception. And oftentimes this inherently led to the concepts of class dynamics and racism. This is a film that is quite frankly begging for this level of interrogation. And the overwhelming majority of people simply don’t care enough to analyse how the film made them feel the way it did or what it has to say about the context in which the film was made in.

Fernando Meirelles stopped caring about being vocal about crime and poverty once he got the check, and I wouldn't have guessed otherwise. I find this film similar to La Haine in political and contextual terms, but one death in La Haine made me think for days, whereas there is a death every minute in City of God. It's not nearly as moving because the characters have no depth. Every person and the city are reduced to their worst, and it was painful to sit through this viewing. I guess the illusion of fatalism masquerading as social critique is too strong to break.

"City of God" is a technically good film that succeeds where many others fail in its ability to seamlessly connect stories, past and present into one cohesive timeline—though oversimplistically. The cinematography is strange, for better or worse, and the color grading or film (whatever it is) looks good at times, but bad in some scenes. Finally, the acting is mostly great. Unfortunately, "City of God" doesn't want to be anything more than this, instead it's an empty action film with pretty technicalities. What pisses me off the most is that that could have been it—a harmless action movie, it was okay, fun even. Sadly, it's based on a true story about a real town that was experiencing significant gang violence in a country where gang violence was and still is a major problem. The movie so badly wants you to care about the protagonist who's difficult life was largely glossed over in the prologue. I'm supposed to feel a dopamine release as both gangs fight to kill eachother faster, and eventually kill themselves too. This could have been interesting, but it's surface level. Back and forth, betrayal, murder, betrayal, murder. That's all it is—I've summed up the movie. What of the people who live in the city? I don't care about the dude who's family was slaughtered; the movie doesn't want to tell me about them. Instead I should focus on his half hearted revenge arc against the other gang. The movie tries to make you feel the brutality of everything, but you won't. It's all fake. And I just don't believe that the director wanted it to be any other way. He's too cool with it all, and I'm convinced that it's meant to be so—like a fairytale, not a real tragedy, or an on-going problem. An isolated story with an all too happy ending is what we get. Violence continues onto the next generation, but it feels half-hearted, like the director wanted to make a Hollywood blockbuster; small touches of artificial humanity are only put there to make the audience emotional. Characters are empty, blank slates. Poor characterization makes Rocket feel indifferent at times. Mega glorification of all that's bad.

The movie itself is incredibly graphic, but there is a purpose behind it. It shows the violence and hatred that happens when that is all you know, but there is something deep inside us, call it science, human phycology, or a conscience that wonders if there is more to life than fear, rage, and brutality. I did think that was a good message to show that violence doesn’t solve violence. Revenge doesn’t bring satisfaction, peace or closure. Hate cannot solve hate. This messaging however is what it felt like it was trying to say but I was trying to find the moral of this all. Was the purpose of this movie was to tell the loose true story of the characters? The environment and culture of Rio during this time? I felt a bit lost and that messaging I said about hate cannot solving hate was something I had to pull like teeth. Good message? Yes. Hard to find it however. Did I think the of the nudity needed to be in it? No. Since it was a common cinematography and lighting technique to have lots of the violent and graphic acts be done in shadows or heavily implied, I believe the nudity scenes should have followed that same rule of thumb. Imply it. You don’t need the full on images of it unless it tells a story. The consistency of that style of filmmaking didn’t match up with the graphic natures. Another thing about the cinematography was rough. It was shaky in pretty much every single shot and there were SO MANY QUICK shots back to back to back in literal second. It was rough. I had a headache the first few minutes of watching this film and it was the same style for the entire film. It was exhausting and made it difficult to not only follow along, but read the dialogue as well. Not the best choices when it came to film editing.

I've wanted to watch this for years and years, and yet I never did. Maybe there was a reason for that. City of God brims with flair and technique, and there is nary a moment when the image and sound presented aren't well rendered and constructed. But therein lies the issue with this film. It feels too constructed, too amalgamated. The result of a heap of story material set ablaze specifically to hide from sincerity. Is the story true? To a turn, as many of these kinds of stories are. I think where this one falters is that it never seems to stop to consider that it's got one foot in the door of stylized imaginings of a roughly relatable cinematic narrative, and the other in the door of gritty depiction of the lives of the sub-altern. It tends to choose style more than anything else, and in doing so leaves a lot on the table. The flair and flash of its photography, cutting and acting lose quite a bit of their impact by the time you see the 15th or so callous murder--a weightlessness that it feels like the film encourages after a fashion. Simply put: there isn't enough story behind the pomp and circumstance to keep the style engaging. The narrative feels less like a cohesive tableau and more like a series of loosely connected vignettes that are united by violence and excess and not by character presence or investment. Glad I watched it, but I can't say I'm happy with what I watched.

City of God is executed with such technical skill that it almost feels like exhibitionism on the filmmakers’ part. We get split-screens, we get sharply edited montages, we get scenes shown twice from different perspectives, and we get some long, magnificent tracking shots, often through crowds, that must have been almost impossible to pull off. It’s really slick. But what is it? Is it a brutal gangster flick, or a social drama about degradation that carries genuine anthropological weight? The easy answer would be to say it’s both, and the vast swathes of critics and fans who think the movie’s terrific would be sure to express such a sentiment. I’m not so sure. Especially in its second hour, I felt the movie leaned more heavily toward the first description than the second, as its plot became denser and its level of sensationalist violence intensified. Thematically, and often in execution, too, it’s very similar to the TV show The Wire, and I can’t be the first to point that out, though contemporary critics would not have had the luxury of such a comparison. Inevitably, it is not able to say as much in two hours as The Wire was able to say over five seasons and fifty episodes. But, for one thing, The Wire breathed human life into its antagonists, and showed us that their actions are not always motivated by greed or viciousness. This cannot be said for City of God’s principal villain Lil Ze, who laughingly dispatches crying children on-camera and for whom passing jealousy is a perfectly good motive to rape a stranger while making her boyfriend watch. Sympathetic characters- Benny, for example, or Rocket, are conveniently never shown engaging in violent acts at all; we are left in no doubt which characters we are supposed to like and which characters we aren’t. Subsequently, it lacks The Wire’s more complex, incisive dynamics. On a cinema screen in 2002, when here in the UK I was still technically not old enough to watch it, it might have been pretty wild. Oldboy too. But though I did prefer it to Oldboy, ultimately I felt that, with its swathes of characters, its whip-smart edits, its proliferating abundance of death and carnage, the film was using sensory overload in an attempt to steamroller me into exhilaration. As it is, on a small screen 20 years later, I don’t feel the film had the kind of power that it appeared to be striving for. It’s not a bad film- far from it. It’s actually a very good one if the material happens to resonate with you. But what does it have to tell us, really, other than that the slums of Rio are terrible beyond belief, where the police have no power, and where the most amoral of a given generation tend to be the ones that rise up through the ranks and end up essentially running the place? I don’t know, really. That does seem to be the main heft of the piece. And there’s a titillating aspect to City of God that sits uncomfortably with its apparent status as a social document, a ‘message from the front line’. Towards the end of the movie I grew tired of the back and forth between the gang violence, which felt repetitive and held back the pacing. After a while, you started seeing things the same way. The cinematography was also really cool and effective. Particularly liked the club scene. Why not 5 stars? I mean I just didn’t ‘wow’ me as much as some of the 5 star movies I have. The thing is, I won’t see gang films or films about poverty the same after this, because I think it’s the most accurate portrayal of those themes ever (that also happens to be entertaining). This movie reminded me a bit of The Infierno, where the cycle of violence never truly ends—it just gets passed on to the next generation. In City of God, though, the city was literally lawless, so the violence didn't have to wait for one generation to die before continuing. The ambition and brutality were simply passed from one group of kids in the favela to the next. Li'l Zé is one of the most despicable, disgusting, and pathetic characters I've ever seen in a movie. The fact that the film reveals at the end that it's based on a true story hit me hard. People like that are out there. Even though he's a victim of the environment he grew up in, I don't feel any sympathy for him—not even when he was a child. He seemed to have the personality of a psychopath from the very beginning. It's incredible that Bené genuinely enjoyed the company of someone as pathetic as Zé. Not even his death made me feel any better because that rain of bullets wasn't nearly enough punishment for all the pain and terror he caused. Talking about the movie itself, I understand why it's considered a masterpiece. It certainly was for me too. I'm not new to this kind of non-chronological storytelling, but saving the opening scene until the last 15 minutes of the movie felt incredible. I thought it was going to be a Casino situation, where the opening scene doesn't come back until about an hour and a half into the film.

Proof that the cameraman really never dies… LMAO On a real note, this is an absolute masterpiece. From the cinematography to the acting to the pacing, it is as close to perfection as a film can get. I spent a good 45 minutes after finishing it trying to come up with a single complaint, and not one thing came to mind. From the opening sequence with its incredible 360° transition and beautifully composed still shots to the emotionally devastating ending framed from behind, City of God is one of the best movies I’ve ever seen and, dare I say, the most creatively executed. There are so many things to love about this movie, but after doing my due diligence and learning that roughly 70% of the cast consisted of local children with little or no acting experience, I appreciated it even more. It makes the performances feel that much more authentic. It’s hard to write a review when there are so many aspects deserving of praise, but one thing I have to highlight is how interconnected the story is. There are at least 25 meaningful characters, yet somehow every single one leaves an impression. It doesn’t matter how much screen time they have—their presence is remembered and their role in the story feels important. I’d compare it to The Godfather , another film with an enormous cast, but I actually think City of God handles its ensemble even better. Every storyline feels purposeful, and none of the characters get lost in the chaos. I could easily write four more paragraphs about this film, but to keep it short, if you asked me to describe it in one sentence, I’d simply say it’s as close to a perfect film as I’ve ever seen. “Wanna get shot in the hand or the foot?” 9.9/10
